- No stacking.
- Uses **color divergence** (blue to orange/red) to distinguish cooler vs. warmer values.

- **Top:** Diverging vertical **bar chart** (time series bars around a zero baseline).
- **Bottom:** **Choropleth-style world map** / gridded heat map of temperature anomaly.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Two-panel vertical layout**: a bar chart above a world map.
- No faceting or small multiples.
- No stacking.
- Uses **color divergence** (blue to orange/red) to distinguish cooler vs. warmer values.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year | Temporal | Position on x-axis in the top bar chart; text label for 2019 |
| Global average temperature difference relative to the middle of the 20th century | Quantitative | Position/length of bars from zero baseline in the top chart; bar color (blue for negative, orange for positive) |
| Geographic location (world grid / latitude-longitude region) | Spatial | Position on the map |
| Temperature difference in 2019 relative to the middle of the 20th century | Quantitative | Color/hue on the map (blue to red scale) |
| No data status | Categorical/nominal | White fill in the map legend / map cells |

raw_comment: As the reveal pointed out, the average temperatures for each year are becoming much more extreme, and much more varying year to year. raw_comment: Before seeing the graph, I had expected a pretty notable change between the rise of temperatures over the year, but was not expecting at all this drastic of an increase. When people in school or even out of school, used to bring up the topic of global warming, I honestly didn't think twice about it. I thought they were more of making guesses, or had very little evidence but I  was very wrong. If global warming keeps rising at this rapid rate, the outcome will soon be horrendous. We need to start taking action against this as we are huge contributors to the heat. Burning fossil fuels to generate energy is the main source of heat-trapping emissions, generating about two billion tons of CO2 per year. If we could just start by trying to use more and more different energy sources such as hydro electricity or wind power, then we would be able to notice a huge change in the temperature drop.

raw_comment: I am glad the New York Times used decade long averages/a times series graph because that eliminates random environmental events. When first looking at the graph, I didn't necessarily know what the baseline was. The reveal states that it is the average between 1951-1980. That information helps to put the graph into perspective. Now looking at it, the designers probably used 1951-1980 because of the fluctuations between negative and positive in that area. From there, it is easier to understand the rest of the graph. All the information in the reveal helps me to understand how serious this situation actually is. Warming by even a degree since the 19th century will have devastating effects on the environment and its creatures.

And that’s only if the global average temperature increases by 1 degree Celsius! Mr. Yohe thinks the temperature could increase another 3.

- **Top:** Diverging vertical **bar chart** (time series bars around a zero baseline).
- **Bottom:** **Choropleth-style world map** / gridded heat map of temperature anomaly.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Two-panel vertical layout**: a bar chart above a world map.
- No faceting or small multiples.
- No stacking.
- Uses **color divergence** (blue to orange/red) to distinguish cooler vs. warmer values.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year | Temporal | Position on x-axis in the top bar chart; text label for 2019 |
| Global average temperature difference relative to the middle of the 20th century | Quantitative | Position/length of bars from zero baseline in the top chart; bar color (blue for negative, orange for positive) |
| Geographic location (world grid / latitude-longitude region) | Spatial | Position on the map |
| Temperature difference in 2019 relative to the middle of the 20th century | Quantitative | Color/hue on the map (blue to red scale) |
| No data status | Categorical/nominal | White fill in the map legend / map cells |

raw_comment:
The reveal showed that we may be too far gone already. This decade has been the hottest by quite a bit, and this year has been the second warmest in recent times. This upward trend may already be too difficult to stop, especially with funding having to be directed towards the various natural disasters that will keep happening. The massive storms, fires, and the pandemic are not helping in the effort to produce less emissions, despite the pandemic seemingly reducing the amount of pollution in the short term. In reality, so much money that could be allocated towards green energy is instead being rerouted towards small businesses that are suffering without business. 

The planet's fever may be too severe already, and the little bit of Tylenol that we're giving isn't enough to change what we've already done.

raw_comment:
Before the reveal, I did not understand how great the temperature rise was. I saw that there had been an increase and saw it as a sign of global warming. However, I did not fully comprehend how great of an increase 1 degree celsius was. After reading the article in the reveal, "Why Half a Degree of Global Warming is a Big Deal, I now understand why 1 celsius can make a huge difference. 
        An increase of 1 celsius might not even be something we would notice. We would sit in our air-conditioned houses ignoring the rising temperatures. However, many organisms in the world are temperature-sensitive. For example, to corals, a half a degree of celsius can mean their lives. Corals have photosynthetic that live on them, feed them, and give them color. However, if temperatures rise by as little as half a degree, these algae will leave the coral because they cannot stand the high temperatures. I learned that this is true for many other organisms as well. The reveal showed me how crucial it is to take action on climate change now, because if we do not reverse our actions soon, it could be too late.

raw_comment:
As I suspected, the rise in temperatures as the years have gone on is directly related to environmental issues, such as the Australian wildfires, melting sea ice in the Antarctic, and the Caribbean hurricanes. I'm unsure of what the Day Zero water shortages are, but I'll be sure to research that later. I'm curious as to why the New York Times chose now to publish a graph like this, when there could be many other interesting graphs chosen during a time like this.
I think a good idea would be for New York Times to explain why the 1940s had such an increase in temperatures than in previous years. In my previous comment, I contributed that to WWII, but I would also just like to really know why it is red. Besides that, I think this graph shows one truth about humans and the world. We must do more to save our environment. If we do not, the temperatures will only continue to rise, and we will harm our environment even more than we already have.

- **Top:** Diverging vertical **bar chart** (time series bars around a zero baseline).
- **Bottom:** **Choropleth-style world map** / gridded heat map of temperature anomaly.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Two-panel vertical layout**: a bar chart above a world map.
- No faceting or small multiples.
- No stacking.
- Uses **color divergence** (blue to orange/red) to distinguish cooler vs. warmer values.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year | Temporal | Position on x-axis in the top bar chart; text label for 2019 |
| Global average temperature difference relative to the middle of the 20th century | Quantitative | Position/length of bars from zero baseline in the top chart; bar color (blue for negative, orange for positive) |
| Geographic location (world grid / latitude-longitude region) | Spatial | Position on the map |
| Temperature difference in 2019 relative to the middle of the 20th century | Quantitative | Color/hue on the map (blue to red scale) |
| No data status | Categorical/nominal | White fill in the map legend / map cells |

dependency_graph.sentence: The map does a better job of showing where the biggest increases in temperature have occurred.

depends_on.justification: (1) B contrasts with A by favoring the map instead of the graph for a different purpose. (2) Contrastive because it sets up a comparison that pulls against A's preference rather than elaborating it.

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 2c: Compares the map's spatial pattern of increases across locations.

dependency_graph.sentence: With the map, we can have a better view of what is being affected the most by the increase in temperature.

depends_on.justification: (1) B follows from the map's ability to show where increases occurred by stating what can be seen from it. (2) Inferential because it draws a consequence about understanding the affected areas, not just adding detail.

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 2c: Describes a spatial pattern of affected areas visible in the map.

dependency_graph.sentence: Our actions are causing so many disturbances.

depends_on.justification: (1) B generalizes from the temperature increase causing harm in A to human actions causing disturbances. (2) Inferential because it extends the causal idea into a broader claim, not a mere elaboration.

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 6: Attributes disturbances to human actions, which is causal reasoning.

dependency_graph.sentence: We sometimes do not even realize it.

depends_on.justification: (1) B elaborates on the disturbances caused by our actions in A by noting our lack of awareness. (2) Elaborative because it adds contextual commentary on the same issue rather than a new causal or evaluative claim.

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 7: Standalone claim about human awareness, not directly shown in the chart.

dependency_graph.sentence: 2019 was the second warmest year since the data was last collected.

dependency_graph.sentence: We need to take that information into consideration.

depends_on.justification: (1) B uses the 2019 temperature fact in A as a reason for action. (2) Inferential because it turns the observation into a recommendation, not a simple elaboration.

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 4a: 'Need to' is a deontic operator prescribing action.

dependency_graph.sentence: We need to try and figure out what we are doing wrong.

depends_on.justification: (1) B follows from the need to consider the 2019 information in A by calling for diagnosis of our mistakes. (2) Inferential because it proposes a next step based on the prior claim, not a refinement.

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 4a: 'Need to' prescribes action and implies correction.

dependency_graph.sentence: We have been doing wrong.

depends_on.justification: (1) B restates the idea of doing wrong in a more direct form. (2) Elaborative because it reinforces the same point rather than adding a new causal or evaluative dimension.

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 4a: Moral judgment that something is wrong, functioning as a prescriptive critique.

dependency_graph.sentence: Some generations are leaving behind such a large carbon footprint.

depends_on.justification: (1) B specifies the kind of harmful human action alluded to in A. (2) Inferential because it introduces a concrete causal contributor to the disturbances, not just a detail.

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 7: General factual claim about carbon footprints, not directly read from the chart.

dependency_graph.sentence: We need to find a way to bring that down.

depends_on.justification: (1) B follows from the large carbon footprint in A by calling for reduction. (2) Inferential because it states an action response to the problem, not an elaboration.

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 4a: 'Need to' is a prescriptive call for action.

dependency_graph.sentence: We need to save the places and animals in danger due to our actions.

depends_on.justification: (1) B specifies the harmed places and animals implied by the disturbances in A. (2) Inferential because it states a consequence of our actions and a resulting need, rather than merely elaborating.

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 4a: 'Need to' prescribes action to protect places and animals.

dependency_graph.sentence: We need to preserve this world for our future generations.

depends_on.justification: (1) B broadens the preservation goal from the endangered places and animals in A to the world for future generations. (2) Inferential because it extends the action recommendation into a larger consequence-oriented claim.

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 4a: 'Need to' is a direct prescription for action.

dependency_graph.sentence: The human population should thrive.

depends_on.justification: (1) B states a broader desired outcome that motivates preserving the world in A. (2) Inferential because it gives a normative end-state that follows from the preservation claim.

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 4a: 'Should' is a deontic operator expressing what ought to happen.

dependency_graph.sentence: We should not destroy a world that has given us so much.

depends_on.justification: (1) B is a normative judgment reinforcing the preservation claim in A. (2) Evaluative because it expresses a moral stance about what we should do, rather than a factual consequence or elaboration.

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 4a: 'Should not' is a prescriptive moral judgment about what ought not to happen.

raw_comment: As I looked at the reveal, I realized that my assumption was correct. The temperature changes and some of the trends were caused by human activities. We’ve really left our footprint on the globe. The stat nuggets also showed a trend that’s been happening since the 1960’s. Each decade, the globe gets noticeably warmer and the 2010’s was no exception. The amount of red (the more the temperature has gone up) on the globe increased significantly, especially around the polar ice caps. Alaska is running out of ice, and they’ve just had their hottest month in July 2019. Australia is also struggling with temperature changes in that they are having their worst fire season on record. South Africa is about to hit a problem with access to electricity as water levels get lower and the drought gets worse. I wonder how many more problems global warming can cause for us? A fix seems very far away.

## 1) Chart type
- **Top:** Diverging vertical **bar chart** (time series bars around a zero baseline).
- **Bottom:** **Choropleth-style world map** / gridded heat map of temperature anomaly.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Two-panel vertical layout**: a bar chart above a world map.
- No faceting or small multiples.
- No stacking.
- Uses **color divergence** (blue to orange/red) to distinguish cooler vs. warmer values.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year | Temporal | Position on x-axis in the top bar chart; text label for 2019 |
| Global average temperature difference relative to the middle of the 20th century | Quantitative | Position/length of bars from zero baseline in the top chart; bar color (blue for negative, orange for positive) |
| Geographic location (world grid / latitude-longitude region) | Spatial | Position on the map |
| Temperature difference in 2019 relative to the middle of the 20th century | Quantitative | Color/hue on the map (blue to red scale) |

raw_comment:
Looking at this graph,what I notice first is how steadily the temperatures are increasing, a little over .25 degrees every 20 years, but the amounts it increases by is still going up at each increment. But there was an odd temperature fluctuation in 1940 and afterwards temperatures switched between colder and warmer before the steady incline of hot temperatures starting around 1980 to the highest it’s ever been in the 2016-2019 range. 

The second image, the map, what immediately jumps out at me is how overwhelmingly orange the map is, mith a decent amount of red. There’s barely any blue at all, and unfortunately most of the red is congregated up in the arctic, which doesn’t surprise me due to how much the polar ice caps have melted in even just the last decade. 

A few things I wonder, are why was the global temperature fluctuating so much from 1940 to 1980? Why on the map have a few areas gotten colder, what’s different about those places? And what is being done to combat global warming across the globe.

raw_comment:
“Is technology doing more harm than good?”

It’s clear to me from looking at this graph that the 80s haven’t exactly been easy on the global average temperature. I can see that as the years go by, the average temperature is moving up in increments of .25. This has already happened three times in the last 39 years and I wouldn’t be surprised if we hit the +1 degree Celsius mark in the next year or so. For anyone who doesn’t believe in global warming, this graph is a pretty clear sign that it’s real and started in the 80s with the invention of the internet. 

Even though the first Industrial Revolution had started before the graph’s x-axis’ shows, the fact that the columns were still in the blue zone after that and even through the second Industrial Revolution reveals just how bad our problem is today. We shouldn’t be having a higher increase in global temperature than what was happening during the Industrial Revolutions when factory regulation was limited. 

Looking at the world map, I can see that almost every single place on earth has experienced a recent increase in temperature. Sure it’s been almost a hundred years since the 50s, but the Arctic regions of the world shouldn’t have such significant temperature differences. Regions like Alaska and parts of Russia have had increases up to 3 degrees Celsius! We need to take a step back and decide if mass producing technology is the best for the earth in the long run.

- **Top:** Diverging vertical **bar chart** (time series bars around a zero baseline).
- **Bottom:** **Choropleth-style world map** / gridded heat map of temperature anomaly.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Two-panel vertical layout**: a bar chart above a world map.
- No faceting or small multiples.
- No stacking.
- Uses **color divergence** (blue to orange/red) to distinguish cooler vs. warmer values.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year | Temporal | Position on x-axis in the top bar chart; text label for 2019 |
| Global average temperature difference relative to the middle of the 20th century | Quantitative | Position/length of bars from zero baseline in the top chart; bar color (blue for negative, orange for positive) |
| Geographic location (world grid / latitude-longitude region) | Spatial | Position on the map |
| Temperature difference in 2019 relative to the middle of the 20th century | Quantitative | Color/hue on the map (blue to red scale) |
| No data status | Categorical/nominal | White fill in the map legend / map cells |

- **Top:** Diverging vertical **bar chart** (time series bars around a zero baseline).
- **Bottom:** **Choropleth-style world map** / gridded heat map of temperature anomaly.

- **Two-panel vertical layout**: a bar chart above a world map.
- No faceting or small multiples.
- No stacking.
- Uses **color divergence** (blue to orange/red) to distinguish cooler vs. warmer values.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year | Temporal | Position on x-axis in the top bar chart; text label for 2019 |
| Global average temperature difference relative to the middle of the 20th century | Quantitative | Position/length of bars from zero baseline in the top chart; bar color (blue for negative, orange for positive) |
| Geographic location (world grid / latitude-longitude region) | Spatial | Position on the map |
| Temperature difference in 2019 relative to the middle of the 20th century | Quantitative | Color/hue on the map (blue to red scale) |
| No data status | Categorical/nominal | White fill in the map legend / map cells |

raw_comment: The graph shows the change in earths average temperature over about a century and a half. This graph is both scary and reassuring to me. At first glance it seems as if our world is melting away at our finger tips and that (according to the graph) we are to far gone to even correct this course. However, with a little bit of study, this graph has some silver lining. First, the changes are miniscule. This is not to say they aren't important but a 1/4 degree change is a lot easier to reverse than a 4 degree change. Also, more importantly, the beginning of the graph shows the earth being much cooler than the average. Now, I don't know if this is just because the average is being dragged up by our current situation but it seems (from this graph) to be a pattern that resembles a wave getting closer and closer to equilibrium. But hey, what do I know?

raw_comment:
In today's age, most people either know or have heard of global warming. They know that the Earth is getting warmer but they don't know exactly the exact reason why. In this graph, other than the obvious increase in temperature over time, I first noticed the variation in temperatures between the years. From 1880-1940 I expected the temperature to gradually increase at an even rate but it didn't. During that time, industrialization was just starting to appear but it seems that nature took its course. However, things changed in 1940 most likely because of World War II. After a period of switching between colder and warmer temperatures, the world started a trend of getting dramatically warmer. The highest peak of warming today almost triples the average temperature of the past. Because of the number of people and supplies we need to sustain ourselves, we are putting a strains on the Earth. Nowadays, people are starting to take notice of our actions because of the impacts they will have on our future. Even my friends at school are starting to protest. However, I still have many questions that I want to be answered. Specifically, referring to the graph, I wonder is why from 1940-1980 the average temperature kept switching between negative and positive? The last thing I wonder is since the average temperatures of today triple that of the past, how much warmer can it get before even more problems emerge? 

"Temperatures Go Up Up Up With No Way Down"

raw_comment:
Thanks to all students who responded.  We had so many great catchy headlines that capture the main ideas of the graphs:  “"Temperatures Go Up Up Up With No Way Down" by Akye of Hoggard High School in Wilmington, North Carolina, “Planet Overheating” by Lily of Seoul, South Korea, “In Flux Because Of Us: How We Control Our Planet's Climate” by Ms. Keohane’s 8th Grade  in Lafayette, California , and "The Proof of Global Warming - Are We the Cause?" by Gabrielle of Ohio.

You can continue to post responses.  Please check back on Friday to see the Reveal with a link to the original New York Times article, some questions about the graph, and a few Stat Nuggets.

image_description:
## 1) Chart type
- **Top:** Diverging vertical **bar chart** (time series bars around a zero baseline).
- **Bottom:** **Choropleth-style world map** / gridded heat map of temperature anomaly.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Two-panel vertical layout**: a bar chart above a world map.
- No faceting or small multiples.
- No stacking.
- Uses **color divergence** (blue to orange/red) to distinguish cooler vs. warmer values.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year | Temporal | Position on x-axis in the top bar chart; text label for 2019 |
| Global average temperature difference relative to the middle of the 20th century | Quantitative | Position/length of bars from zero baseline in the top chart; bar color (blue for negative, orange for positive) |
| Geographic location (world grid / latitude-longitude region) | Spatial | Position on the map |
| Temperature difference in 2019 relative to the middle of the 20th century | Quantitative | Color/hue on the map (blue to red scale) |
| No data status | Categorical/nominal | White fill in the map legend / map cells |

## 1) Chart type
- **Top:** Diverging vertical **bar chart** (time series bars around a zero baseline).
- **Bottom:** **Choropleth-style world map** / gridded heat map of temperature anomaly.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Two-panel vertical layout**: a bar chart above a world map.
- No faceting or small multiples.
- No stacking.
- Uses **color divergence** (blue to orange/red) to distinguish cooler vs. warmer values.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year | Temporal | Position on x-axis in the top bar chart; text label for 2019 |
| Global average temperature difference relative to the middle of the 20th century | Quantitative | Position/length of bars from zero baseline in the top chart; bar color (blue for negative, orange for positive) |
| Geographic location (world grid / latitude-longitude region) | Spatial | Position on the map |
| Temperature difference in 2019 relative to the middle of the 20th century | Quantitative | Color/hue on the map (blue to red scale) |
| No data status | Categorical/nominal | White fill in the map legend / map cells |

raw_comment: The first thing that I noticed is that when looking at the first graph is that global temperatures between 1880-1980 fluctuated between warm and cold consistently, although we were well into the Age of Industrialization at this point. Another thing I noticed was that in the second graph, the most extreme temperature change was in the arctic regions. raw_comment: What I notice when looking at the first graph is that the average global temperatures taken from 1950 to 1981 are used as the relative average global temperature for comparison to the average global temperatures before and after it.  One important thing I notice from this graph is that the average temperatures before 1950 to 1981, specifically from 1880 to 1940 are not only consistently lower than the average temperatures from 1950 to 1981, but there aren’t any specific trends or noticeable shifts in the temperatures, as they tend to hover around an average. On the other hand I notice a specific trend from the years that come after 1980, being a consistent increase in global temperatures each year, and the rate of increase in temperatures, especially approaching 2019, seem to resemble almost an exponential rate.  I believe this shows that global warming isn’t natural because unlike the average temperatures in the past that show little sign of any rate of increase, even with small fluctuations year to year, the trends we are seeing in the graph aren’t just small fluctuations, but large trends that don’t seem to be stopping.  The question I have, and something I wonder from seeing these trends is what efforts will it take to halt the trend we are seeing, and what will the future look like if nothing is done about it?

I notice that the temperature was below the midline until 1939, the year World War ll started. I also noticed it stayed above until around 1945, the year World War ll ended. In this time there was a lot of industrial work that involved fossil fuels to manufacture all the weapons and vehicles used in the horrific war. After the war everything slowed back down and started going back to normal until manufacturers started making more and more things.
By the 1970's things started ramping up when it came to fossil fuels. The Vietnam war just ended allowing more people to be at home and more people looking for work in factories. Manufacturing and the use of fossil fuels is warming the earth more and more as time goes on. The only question is when will the curve flatten out, and will it be too late?

raw_comment: I notice that there is a bit of fluctuation from 1940 to about 1980. This was the start of the steady rise in global temperatures.  This didn't seem like a problem until 1940.  In today's society we all know that the world is getting hotter. There are many reasons that the temperature is increasing, like in the 1950s when everyone was using hairspray, or the large amounts of C02 emitted from cars and large factories. When the production of all of these things were made and used "in bulk" they didn't necessarily know the negative effects of it. From the start of the industrial revolution there has been carbon dioxide buildup. However  CO2 doesn't reach the atmosphere until roughly 10 years later. That means that the problems we are having now are causes from things 10 plus years ago.  When I look at this graph I see the effects of  past events. Yes we may be contributing towards future temperature increase but what we are going through today is not from factories that are pumping out CO2 or cars emitting gas right now. I feel that many people tend to place blame on society today when in reality it was the older generations contributing to the rise in global temperatures.

- **Top:** Diverging vertical **bar chart** (time series bars around a zero baseline).
- **Bottom:** **Choropleth-style world map** / gridded heat map of temperature anomaly.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Two-panel vertical layout**: a bar chart above a world map.
- No faceting or small multiples.
- No stacking.
- Uses **color divergence** (blue to orange/red) to distinguish cooler vs. warmer values.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year | Temporal | Position on x-axis in the top bar chart; text label for 2019 |
| Global average temperature difference relative to the middle of the 20th century | Quantitative | Position/length of bars from zero baseline in the top chart; bar color (blue for negative, orange for positive) |
| Geographic location (world grid / latitude-longitude region) | Spatial | Position on the map |
| Temperature difference in 2019 relative to the middle of the 20th century | Quantitative | Color/hue on the map (blue to red scale) |
| No data status | Categorical/nominal | White fill in the map legend / map cells |

dependency_graph.sentence: This did not seem like a problem until 1940.

depends_on.justification: (1) B reacts to the temperature trend in A by judging when it became problematic. (2) Evaluative because it expresses a subjective assessment rather than a factual elaboration or causal explanation.

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 4a: Uses 'problem' as a normative judgment about the situation.

dependency_graph.sentence: In today's society, we all know that the world is getting hotter.

depends_on.justification: (1) B restates the warming trend in A in a broader present-day framing. (2) Elaborative because it continues the same idea with contextual wording rather than adding a new cause or judgment.

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 7: General background claim about society's knowledge and climate, not directly shown in the chart.

dependency_graph.sentence: There are many reasons that the temperature is increasing.

depends_on.justification: (1) B generalizes from the warming trend in A to the claim that it has multiple causes. (2) Inferential because it moves from observation to explanatory framing rather than simply detailing A.

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 6: Introduces causal reasoning by asserting multiple reasons for the increase.

dependency_graph.sentence: One reason is the use of hairspray in the 1950s.

depends_on.justification: (1) B supplies one of the reasons mentioned in A. (2) Elaborative because it specifies a member of the set of reasons rather than introducing a separate causal chain.

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 6: Proposes a specific cause for the temperature increase.

dependency_graph.sentence: Another reason is the large amounts of C02 emitted from cars and large factories.

depends_on.justification: (1) B supplies another reason mentioned in A. (2) Elaborative because it adds a parallel explanatory detail within the same topic.

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 6: Proposes another causal explanation for the increase.

dependency_graph.sentence: When the production of all of these things was made and used in bulk, people did not necessarily know the negative effects of it.

depends_on.justification: (1) B explains why the hairspray-related production in A was not recognized as harmful at the time. (2) Inferential because it introduces a causal/contextual explanation about awareness, not just more detail.

(1) B explains why the car/factory emissions in A were not necessarily understood as harmful. (2) Inferential because it reasons about historical awareness and consequences rather than elaborating the emissions themselves.

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 7: Background claim about people's knowledge and production practices, not directly shown in the chart.

dependency_graph.sentence: From the start of the industrial revolution, there has been carbon dioxide buildup.

depends_on.justification: (1) B broadens the emissions claim in A into a long-term buildup over time. (2) Inferential because it draws a causal-historical conclusion from the emissions described, not merely restating them.

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 7: Standalone historical/environmental claim not directly shown in the chart.

dependency_graph.sentence: However, CO2 does not reach the atmosphere until roughly 10 years later.

depends_on.justification: (1) B qualifies the buildup claim in A by introducing a delay before atmospheric impact. (2) Contrastive because 'However' marks a tension/qualification rather than a same-direction elaboration.

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 7: General scientific claim stated without explicit linkage to the chart observation.

dependency_graph.sentence: That means that the problems we are having now are causes from things 10 plus years ago.

depends_on.justification: (1) B explicitly draws a conclusion from the delay described in A. (2) Inferential because it states a causal implication about present problems stemming from past actions.

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 6: Links current problems to past causes, making a causal inference.

dependency_graph.sentence: When I look at this graph, I see the effects of past events.

depends_on.justification: (1) B interprets the delayed-cause claim in A as visible effects on the graph. (2) Inferential because it converts the causal explanation into an interpretive conclusion about the data.

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 6: Interprets the chart as showing effects caused by earlier events.

dependency_graph.sentence: We may be contributing towards future temperature increase.

depends_on.justification: (1) B extends the idea of past causes in A into a future-oriented consequence. (2) Inferential because it predicts a further effect rather than elaborating the graph reading.

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 8: Future-oriented hypothetical about possible contribution to later warming.

dependency_graph.sentence: What we are going through today is not from factories that are pumping out CO2 right now.

depends_on.justification: (1) B contrasts with A by denying that current problems come from present-day factories. (2) Contrastive because it pushes against the immediate-cause interpretation and redirects the explanation.

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 6: Causal claim about what is not causing the current situation.

dependency_graph.sentence: What we are going through today is not from cars emitting gas right now.

depends_on.justification: (1) B similarly contrasts with A by denying present-day cars as the source of current problems. (2) Contrastive because it qualifies the causal story in A rather than elaborating it.

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 6: Causal claim about what is not causing the current situation.

dependency_graph.sentence: Many people tend to place blame on society today.

depends_on.justification: (1) B contrasts with A by describing a common but mistaken attribution of blame to the present. (2) Contrastive because it sets up a mismatch between popular blame and the earlier-cause explanation.
(1) B contrasts with A by describing a common but mistaken attribution of blame to the present. (2) Contrastive because it opposes the immediate-cause framing in A.

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 7: Background claim about social attitudes, not directly shown in the chart.

dependency_graph.sentence: In reality, it was the older generations contributing to the rise in global temperatures.

depends_on.justification: (1) B corrects the blame assignment in A by shifting responsibility to older generations. (2) Contrastive because 'In reality' explicitly opposes the prior attribution rather than elaborating it.

raw_comment:
Title: "It's Getting Hot in Here" 

This graph shows the increase in global average temperature. From 1980 to now there has been a 25 degree increase within the 10-15 year range. Clearly there has been an impetus that began the steady increase in temperature around 1980, whether it is more technology, factory production, etc. Before then, the temperature seemed to fluctuate, increasing and decreasing from decade to decade. I wonder if this data is simply due to climate patterns or if there was also a stimulus causing these changes. Also interesting to note that before serious mass production of goods, the global average temperature was always low.

image_description:
## 1) Chart type
- **Top:** Diverging vertical **bar chart** (time series bars around a zero baseline).
- **Bottom:** **Choropleth-style world map** / gridded heat map of temperature anomaly.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Two-panel vertical layout**: a bar chart above a world map.
- No faceting or small multiples.
- No stacking.
- Uses **color divergence** (blue to orange/red) to distinguish cooler vs. warmer values.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year | Temporal | Position on x-axis in the top bar chart; text label for 2019 |
| Global average temperature difference relative to the middle of the 20th century | Quantitative | Position/length of bars from zero baseline in the top chart; bar color (blue for negative, orange for positive) |
| Geographic location (world grid / latitude-longitude region) | Spatial | Position on the map |
| Temperature difference in 2019 relative to the middle of the 20th century | Quantitative | Color/hue on the map (blue to red scale) |
| No data status | Categorical/nominal | White fill in the map legend / map cells |

raw_comment:
Headline: Is that sweat on your face?

What I noticed is that in the 1940s we rose in temperature from World War II. Then we settled down a bit after that but then we kept going up and down through the years. Then eventually we didn't return to the normal temperatures instead we rose and kept going up. As technology advances and the need for energy goes up. People needed resources to produce energy so we built power plants which caused lots of harm. Then somewhere along the line, we needed to trade with other countries. So we put tons of fuel on cargo ships and sent them across the oceans for resources. This also has a great impact on temperature. 

What I wonder is can the human race switch over to a new power source that does not cause any harm? My answer to this question is probably not. Other energy sources are cheaper to maintain and can get more power. Whereas I believe one solar panel that's big enough to run a house is probably around 10,000 dollars. Now I'm not a solar panel expert but they go for a ton of money and normal people can't buy them that easily. We would need people to group together or have powerful people to build their own solar panel factories and sell that power to the people. But, sadly people usually go for the cheaper option because in our society money is power. So this dream might never happen unless governments acknowledge this threat and start doing things necessary to stop the temperature from rising.

raw_comment:
Two words pop into my head the second I see this graph. Global warming. Some say that preventive measures need to be taken to solve this problem and some don’t care to even acknowledge its existence, but either way, you can’t argue with statistics. 

I noticed that the average global temperature between 1880-1940 stayed below the midline. Industrialization had just begun. But, in 1940, the graph shows a spike in the average temperature for a couple of years. This makes me wonder how the effects of WWII (maximized industrial production, vehicle exhaust, bombs, etc.) could've caused the temperature to rise. Afterall, coal was still the world’s primary energy source which was essential to electricity, production and manufacturing, and transport. The graph shows that the temperature danced above and below the midline until just a couple years before 1980 (probably due to the industrialization of many other countries and the aftermath of WWII). Ever since 1980, the temperature has been constantly above the midline and is well on the rise with no sign of dropping again. 

I wonder if we'll ever really be able to slow the effects of global warming. We rely on fossil fuels in our day to day lives for transportation, heating, electricity, and for many other industrial applications. It isn’t like we can just stop using them. However, a gradual decrease of using fossil fuels and a gradual increase of using renewable energy should be something to think about as we go about the future.

raw_comment:
Climbing Temperatures, No Way Down

Climate change is a very hot topic in today's day and age. Even with a pandemic going on outside, some of the most frequent news that I see is "Global temperature rises to decrease by 6% this year. Is that enough to reverse our climate crisis?" It's difficult to understand such a broad topic, but I found this graph very informative and interesting.

The first thing that I notice is that when this graph starts, in 1880, the temperatures weren't the coldest. In fact, it wasn't until about 23 years later that temperatures finally reached their all time low. Another thing that I notice is that between the years of 1935-1980, temperatures are, more or less, fluctuating along the centerline. I wonder if there are any patterns or reasons behind why the temperatures in this period fluctuated like they did. Something else that I notice is that after 1980, when temperatures started steadily increasing, they went up very quickly. Based on the numbers on the graph, temperatures have gone up almost .75 degrees from 1980. In only 40 years, our global temperature increased by much more than it ever has in the past, based on this graph. I wonder what practices we implemented to cause temperatures to go up so drastically, and if those practices are avoidable. Climate change has been a concern of mine for some time now, and I considered myself very knowledgeable on it, but this graph opened my eyes to what is really happening to our planet, and it's scary.

raw_comment:
Headline: Rising Temperatures Linked to Growth of Industrialism
        I notice in the graph that global temperatures were over .25 degrees Celsius lower than average in many years from 1880 to 1930. Around 1940, temperatures saw a short spike above average. In the following years, readings fluctuated above and below average. Then, around 1978, temperatures skyrocketed, rising each year to almost 1 degree Celsius higher than average at current. These temperature changes are indicative of the presence of global warming and show the enormous effect modern industrialization has had. 
        In the 1880s until the 1940s, temperatures were lower than average almost every year. During this time, industrialization was beginning in many countries. Factories had begun spewing greenhouse gases into the atmosphere. The effect of these rapidly accumulating gases was not seen until temperatures began to fluctuate above and below average around 1940. Modern industrialization continued and gases like carbon dioxide and methane kept entering the air. As a result, temperatures started increasing steadily in 1980. Since then, every year has been above average temperature. New temperature records are now set often. Yet environmentally friendly growth has not happened. People continue to use the same devices that have caused this increase in temperature. I can only wonder if the world will ever decide to stop catastrophe by lowering greenhouse gas emissions.

raw_comment:
Headline: It's Getting Hot in Here

I notice that the average global temperature has drastically increased since the mid-20th century. Around 1978, the average temperature never fell below the line. raw_comment:
Hearing the phrase global warming is almost common right now everyone is in a panic about it or they act as if nothing is wrong. Looking at the graph I noticed that it wasn't until the 1940s when there was a spike in the global temperature, you can then see that after the spike temperatures attempted to level out but when 1980 came about the temperature rose and didn't come back down. I wonder what activities are going on in the countries that have had their temperatures rise the most, and in the map at the top you can see how the temperature has risen the most. So I wonder why the temperature rose so much in an area that isn't really over a land mass. Though in the 1940s I know that the world was in the midst of World War 2, so I wonder if there is a specific event from the time range that caused the large spike in temperature. Global warming is such a big concern for a lot of people right now, even in my generation I know so many people who are very passionate about the subject and are willing to fight for the cause and protest to get their message across. Even if you don't know much about global warming and what's really going on I feel that we all need to take a step back all look at the picture as a whole, and see that there is a big chance that if we stay on the same path we are on now the temperature may never go back down.

raw_comment:
In today's age, most people either know or have heard of global warming. They know that the Earth is getting warmer but they don't know exactly the exact reason why. In this graph, other than the obvious increase in temperature over time, I first noticed the variation in temperatures between the years. From 1880-1940 I expected the temperature to gradually increase at an even rate but it didn't. During that time, industrialization was just starting to appear but it seems that nature took its course. However, things changed in 1940 most likely because of World War II. After a period of switching between colder and warmer temperatures, the world started a trend of getting dramatically warmer. The highest peak of warming today almost triples the average temperature of the past. Because of the number of people and supplies we need to sustain ourselves, we are putting a strains on the Earth. Nowadays, people are starting to take notice of our actions because of the impacts they will have on our future. Even my friends at school are starting to protest. However, I still have many questions that I want to be answered. Specifically, referring to the graph, I wonder is why from 1940-1980 the average temperature kept switching between negative and positive? The last thing I wonder is since the average temperatures of today triple that of the past, how much warmer can it get before even more problems emerge? 

"Temperatures Go Up Up Up With No Way Down"

raw_comment:
I notice compared to 1880 that the average global temperature has increased by over 1 degree Celsius. This is a bar graph that represents changes in temperatures each year from 1880-2019. The x-axis symbolizes the years and increases by 10 year increments. One bar symbolizes the year in the decade and temperature increase or decrease. The tallest bar above the baseline is the year 2015. The lowest bar below the baseline is in 1903. The main pattern is as the number of years increase, the temperature also increases. The most prominent-looking outlier of the graph is between the years 1939-1945. This was during WWII and inferences can be made that the war equipment and destruction caused the temperature around the world to rise. During WWII, the US had increased the production of high-powered machines such as airplanes and war weapons. The industrial and technological developments caused the temperatures to rise across the globe, as apparent in the map, especially on the poles. These graphs support that waters are also rising by glacier melt.

I wonder if by limiting the industrial and technological developments and minimizing the use of these that exhaust the planet, could the global average temperature decrease back to the baseline? 

Headline: Planet Overheating

Today’s graph and map compare global temperatures for 1880 to 2019 to the average global temperature for mid-20th century (1951 – 1980) .  Note that all temperatures are in degrees Celsius. 
From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?",  "What do you wonder?", and  "What's going on in this graph?"  

Plus, please share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas about the graph and the map. 

On Thursday afternoon, we’ll reveal the article that included these visual representations and much more.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.
Note that you can get a link to your response to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  
“What’s Going On in This Graph?” will be releasing graphs through May!  Please return on Friday for our next graph with moderation on Wednesday, May 6.  The graph – change in the share of U.S. population that is foreign-born.

raw_comment:
"The problems that humans created must be fixed".

It's very obvious by just looking at this graph that the temperature is drastically rising. That is the first thing I noticed, that the temperature is increasing and also that it seems to be increasing exponentially. I wonder if it will continue to increase exponentially or if it will increase in a more linear manner.
Already everyone knows that the reason for global warming is caused by large amounts of burning greenhouse gases. It is no surprise that humans have caused this to happen and it's up to humans to solve the problem. Due to the Coronavirus many people have had to stay at home and quarantine. The world is experiencing a terrible disaster and sadly many people have died. But because of the lowered amount of burned greenhouse gases many places have experienced less pollution. For example, for the first time in decades people who live in India can see the Himalaya mountains. Possibly this is a wake up call to many people that we need to change the way we live and put the earth's needs before our own.

- **Top:** Diverging vertical **bar chart** (time series bars around a zero baseline).
- **Bottom:** **Choropleth-style world map** / gridded heat map of temperature anomaly.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Two-panel vertical layout**: a bar chart above a world map.
- No faceting or small multiples.
- No stacking.
- Uses **color divergence** (blue to orange/red) to distinguish cooler vs. warmer values.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year | Temporal | Position on x-axis in the top bar chart; text label for 2019 |
| Global average temperature difference relative to the middle of the 20th century | Quantitative | Position/length of bars from zero baseline in the top chart; bar color (blue for negative, orange for positive) |
| Geographic location (world grid / latitude-longitude region) | Spatial | Position on the map |
| Temperature difference in 2019 relative to the middle of the 20th century | Quantitative | Color/hue on the map (blue to red scale) |
| No data status | Categorical/nominal | White fill in the map legend / map cells |

dependency_graph.sentence: The problems that humans created must be fixed.
dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 4a: 'Must be fixed' is a deontic prescription about what should happen.

dependency_graph.sentence: It is very obvious by just looking at this graph that the temperature is drastically rising.
dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 2c: Describes a strong upward trend visible in the chart; it is an observation of the data pattern.

dependency_graph.sentence: That is the first thing I noticed.

depends_on.justification: (1) B refers back to the graph observation in A as the first noticed point. (2) Elaborative because it continues the same observation sequence rather than adding a cause or judgment.

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 2: Refers to noticing something in the visualization, but without specifying what was noticed; this is too underspecified to classify meaningfully.

dependency_graph.sentence: The temperature is increasing.

depends_on.justification: (1) B restates the rising temperature described in A in simpler terms. (2) Elaborative because it paraphrases the same factual content rather than introducing new reasoning.

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 2c: Reports an observed increase across the time series.

dependency_graph.sentence: The temperature seems to be increasing exponentially.

depends_on.justification: (1) B builds on the increase in A by characterizing its rate as exponential. (2) Inferential because it goes beyond the basic observation to a stronger pattern claim.

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 2c: Characterizes the overall shape of the trend in the chart as accelerating growth.

dependency_graph.sentence: I wonder if the temperature will continue to increase exponentially.

depends_on.justification: (1) B is a question prompted by the exponential increase in A. (2) Evaluative because it expresses curiosity about the trend rather than explaining it.

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 5: 'I wonder if' expresses uncertainty and a desire for future information.

dependency_graph.sentence: I wonder if the temperature will increase in a more linear manner.

depends_on.justification: (1) B contrasts a possible linear trend with the exponential trend in A and asks about it. (2) Evaluative because it is a subjective question about the pattern, not a factual elaboration.

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 5: This is an explicit question about a possible future pattern.

dependency_graph.sentence: Everyone knows that the reason for global warming is caused by large amounts of burning greenhouse gases.

depends_on.justification: (1) B offers an explanation for the rising temperature observed in A. (2) Inferential because it introduces a causal account rather than merely describing the graph.

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 6: The sentence gives a causal explanation for global warming, linking it to greenhouse gas emissions.

dependency_graph.sentence: Humans have caused this to happen.

depends_on.justification: (1) B identifies humans as the cause of the greenhouse-gas/global-warming mechanism in A. (2) Inferential because it states a causal attribution, not a refinement or reaction.

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 6: Attributes the observed warming to human action, which is causal explanation.

dependency_graph.sentence: It is up to humans to solve the problem.

depends_on.justification: (1) B follows from the human-caused problem in A by assigning responsibility to humans. (2) Inferential because it draws a normative consequence from the causal claim rather than simply evaluating it.

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 4a: 'It is up to humans to solve the problem' assigns responsibility and implies what should be done.

dependency_graph.sentence: Due to the Coronavirus, many people have had to stay at home and quarantine.
dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 7: This is a standalone factual claim about the pandemic, not about the chart's temperature data.

dependency_graph.sentence: The world is experiencing a terrible disaster.

depends_on.justification: (1) B reacts to the coronavirus situation in A by labeling it a terrible disaster. (2) Evaluative because it is a subjective judgment about A, not a factual elaboration or causal explanation.

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 4b: 'Terrible disaster' is an emotional/evaluative reaction without a prescription.

dependency_graph.sentence: Many people have died.

depends_on.justification: (1) B states a severe consequence of the coronavirus situation in A. (2) Inferential because it adds a downstream effect rather than a mere description or judgment.

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 7: Standalone factual claim about deaths, not directly shown in the visualization.

dependency_graph.sentence: Because of the lowered amount of burned greenhouse gases, many places have experienced less pollution.

depends_on.justification: (1) B uses the reduced burning in A as the cause of less pollution. (2) Inferential because it explicitly states a causal consequence, not a refinement.

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 6: 'Because of' links a cause to an observed environmental change, making it explanatory inference.

dependency_graph.sentence: For the first time in decades, people who live in India can see the Himalaya mountains.

depends_on.justification: (1) B gives a concrete environmental effect of the reduced pollution in A. (2) Inferential because it reasons to a new observable outcome rather than elaborating the same claim.

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 7: This is a factual claim about visibility in India, not a chart observation.

dependency_graph.sentence: Possibly this is a wake up call to many people.

depends_on.justification: (1) B reacts to the cleaner-air situation in A by framing it as a wake-up call. (2) Evaluative because it expresses a subjective interpretation rather than a causal explanation.

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 4b: This is an evaluative reaction urging concern, but it does not explicitly prescribe action.

dependency_graph.sentence: We need to change the way we live.

depends_on.justification: (1) B follows from the wake-up-call interpretation in A as a proposed response. (2) Inferential because it turns the prior situation into a prescriptive conclusion.

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 4a: 'Need to' is a clear prescriptive operator.

dependency_graph.sentence: We need to put the earth's needs before our own.

depends_on.justification: (1) B specifies what changing the way we live should mean in A. (2) Elaborative because it refines the same normative idea rather than introducing a new causal or contrastive claim.

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 4a: 'Need to' makes this a normative recommendation.

raw_comment:
Catchy Headline: In Flux Because Of Us: How we control our planet's climate
 
 I notice that in graph one there is no steady or gradual increase of global temperature. It, out of nowhere, began to rise in the 1940’s, but then, in later years it came back down even below where it had been before the surge and was very irregular. I further observed that the first temperature spike was immediately after World War two when there was a boom in new industrialization and factory building. I also noticed that there was a rise in 1980. I believe that the rise in the ‘80s  was due to automobiles becoming something that the average person used around the world, it was also in this time that factory manufacturing became by far the most common way for making goods. Both these things would have caused great influxes in the release of greenhouse gasses which are the primary cause of global warming because they insulate our planet. Since the ‘80s up until now our factory and automobile usage has risen greatly along with our climate and one can assume that it is due to the greenhouse gas emissions.  In the second graph, I notice that the regions with extreme cold climates appear to be the ones with the most significant warming. It also seems that the most developed, populated and industrially advanced places such as China, India and the U.S. that you would assume would emit masses of greenhouse gas, are hardly being affected by rising temperature compared to other regions.

-Caroline Keohane

- **Top:** Diverging vertical **bar chart** (time series bars around a zero baseline).
- **Bottom:** **Choropleth-style world map** / gridded heat map of temperature anomaly.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Two-panel vertical layout**: a bar chart above a world map.
- No faceting or small multiples.
- No stacking.
- Uses **color divergence** (blue to orange/red) to distinguish cooler vs. warmer values.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year | Temporal | Position on x-axis in the top bar chart; text label for 2019 |
| Global average temperature difference relative to the middle of the 20th century | Quantitative | Position/length of bars from zero baseline in the top chart; bar color (blue for negative, orange for positive) |
| Geographic location (world grid / latitude-longitude region) | Spatial | Position on the map |
| Temperature difference in 2019 relative to the middle of the 20th century | Quantitative | Color/hue on the map (blue to red scale) |
| No data status | Categorical/nominal | White fill in the map legend / map cells |

raw_comment:
Reactions and Responses of Gabi Vaculin and Jackson Sander.

We noticed in the map graph, that in the coldest parts of the world like Alaska and the Arctic, the temperature rose the most. We also noticed that from 1980 the temperatures have continued to rise.​
We think that as technology increases, we use more resources, and this causes climate warming.​

We wonder why the temperature rise was highest in a very cold part of the world, Alaska? ​

Title- Graph Fever: It's Rising

raw_comment: The late 1910's and 20's really starts the upward trend of global temperatures. This has to do with the start of mass market commercial industrialization in the United States and Europe. This is best exemplified in the "Roaring Twenties" when American consumers had enough money to buy many products off the factory line. The factories slowed in the thirties due to the Great Depression, but were back up in the 40's due to World War ll. But after that, the temperatures stagnated until the late 70's. And it coincides with the opening of a certain nation. China. Chinese exports really started in the 70's and 80's after the death of Mao Zedong. The aftermath in China led to a massive industrialization effort and a shift to authoritarian capitalism by successive leaders. The upward trend is due to the growing industry in China and India with very few regulations on the environment. This trend will probably continue as many third world countries also start to industrialize in a similar model.

raw_comment:
Global Warming. The Greenhouse Effect. Global Climate Change. Pollution. Ruining The Earth. Whatever you want to call it, it's happening at an irreversible rate. 
Since 1880, the average global temperature has steadily increased, and it seems as though there are no signs of that trend stopping. Once the world began to industrialize and output large quantities of products, emissions caused the global temperature to rise significantly. And as we get closer and closer to modern day, more and more countries are industrializing and contributing to the growing global emissions. How can this be stopped? It may not be able to at this point. We may be too far gone. Are water levels going to rise because of the increase in temperature in the arctic? Are coastal towns and cities doomed to slowly drown? 

This graph and map shows how global temperatures are rising as a result of industrialization, and that is why it should be titled "Industrialization: How it ruined the ecological balance."

raw_comment:
Well, obviously the temperatures on Earth are rising dramatically, but the big question is why? Global warming? Coronavirus? Greenhouse gases? You get the point.
One big point of emphasis that is necessary to look at. 1940. Why is it in red in those years when it is blue before and after those years (well, until the 80s that is). That correlation relates directly with emissions from WWII, and potentially the radiation from the atomic bomb. Why do we see such an increase of red from 1980s on? I personally believe that it can be connected to the development of our lives as an entire world. Countries besides Europe and the US began to prosper, the Cold War was drawing to a close, and war was coming to an end. Countries began to catch up, developing factories (which resulted in emissions into the atmosphere, raising temperatures and sea levels) and infrastructure (construction materials can also hurt the environment).
So, this begs the question. While seeing countries develop and improve the efficiency and technology of our world, at what cost to our environment is this improvement necessary?

Due to COVID-19, we’ve already seen some carbon emissions go down due to a dramatic decrease in travel. Now, organizations will hopefully start to be more active in keeping the exponential increase of global temperature from increasing.

raw_comment:
I notice that this graph shows a dramatic increase in global average temperature since 1980, especially when compared to the average between 1880 and 1940. Obviously, the higher temperatures are depicted with orange and lie above the center line (zero) while  the colder temperatures are depicted in blue and lie below. I also see that over the past 5 years, the average temperature has remained above 0.75 degrees Celsius. In the map, we can see that a majority of areas across the globe are much hotter than they were in the mid 20th century. 

I wonder that why, even with tons of information similar to this, people continue to ignore the issue of a rising global temperature. I am curious about how this pandemic will affect this year's temperature -- Will the degrees Celsius drop because of reduced transit, the shutdown of smaller factories, etc.? Or, will it increase as a result of our greater dependence on home technology? I also wonder if the temperature spike in the 1940's was a result of wartime industrialization, or the weapons used in WWll. 

In these two graphs, we see temperatures rise primarily as a result of human action. I personally would title this graph "The Damage Which We Cause."

sentence_classifications.image_description:
## 1) Chart type
- **Top:** Diverging vertical **bar chart** (time series bars around a zero baseline).
- **Bottom:** **Choropleth-style world map** / gridded heat map of temperature anomaly.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Two-panel vertical layout**: a bar chart above a world map.
- No faceting or small multiples.
- No stacking.
- Uses **color divergence** (blue to orange/red) to distinguish cooler vs. warmer values.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year | Temporal | Position on x-axis in the top bar chart; text label for 2019 |
| Global average temperature difference relative to the middle of the 20th century | Quantitative | Position/length of bars from zero baseline in the top chart; bar color (blue for negative, orange for positive) |
| Geographic location (world grid / latitude-longitude region) | Spatial | Position on the map |
| Temperature difference in 2019 relative to the middle of the 20th century | Quantitative | Color/hue on the map (blue to red scale) |
| No data status | Categorical/nominal | White fill in the map legend / map cells |

The first thing that I noticed when I looked at this graph was the contrast between the left and right side of it. The left side of the graph shows data that’s down in the negative values which, from the late 1800s to 2019, rises to high positive values seen on the right side of the graph. Another thing that I noticed were the different colors used. Anything below the x-axis of the graph is a light blue color while anything above it is an orange/red color. 

After studying the graph, I wonder why they chose to begin using data starting in the 1880s. Why not start before then? (After looking it up it seems as though the second Industrial Revolution began at around this time). I also wonder why there seem to be periods of time around the middle of the graph where the data jumps between being above or below the x-axis. 

All in all, the graph and map is showing the effects of Industrialization on global temperature as it has increased pretty consistently from the late 19th Century to the 21st Century. The map is also showing that places that are generally colder, such as the North and South Pole, are suffering more due to this drastic change in temperature. 

Was More Than One Industrial Revolution Really Necessary?
